label: Yesha'yahu (Isaiah) — 1QIsa-a — Part 5 — Chapters 55–66
summary_plain: Come, everyone who thirsts — come to the waters. You who have no money — come, buy, and eat. YHWH's word goes out and does not return empty. The mountains and hills break forth into singing. YHWH's house shall be called a house of prayer for all peoples. The watchmen are blind, they are all dumb dogs that cannot bark. Is not this the fast that I choose — to loose the bonds of wickedness, to let the oppressed go free? Arise, shine, for your light has come. The Spirit of YHWH is upon me because he has anointed me to bring good news to the afflicted. YHWH creates new heavens and a new earth. The wolf and the lamb shall feed together.
summary_scholarly: The ACR reads from the Great Isaiah Scroll (1QIsa-a) and the Orit Ge'ez. Yesha'yahu 18 (covered in Part 2) resonates through these final chapters — the nations beyond the rivers of Cush are addressed in YHWH's universal restoration plan. Chapter 56:7 declares YHWH's house a 'house of prayer for all peoples' — not for one nation or institution. The fast YHWH chooses (58:6) is justice: releasing the oppressed, feeding the hungry, sheltering the homeless. Chapter 61's anointing passage was read at Qumran (11QMelch) as referring to a mortal herald, not a divine figure. The new heavens and new earth (65:17) is the eschatological hope preserved in the oldest prophetic manuscript.

key_terms.definition: Yesha'yahu 55:1 — 'Come, everyone who thirsts, come to the waters; and he who has no money, come, buy and eat.' YHWH's invitation is free, open to all, and contrasted with what cannot truly satisfy.
Yesha'yahu 56:1-8 explicitly includes foreigners who hold fast to the covenant and eunuchs who keep the Sabbath; they receive a place in YHWH's house better than sons and daughters.

Yesha'yahu 58 contrasts the external fast YHWH rejects with the fast he chooses: loosing bonds of wickedness, letting the oppressed go free, sharing bread with the hungry, bringing the homeless poor into one's house.

key_terms.term: 'The Spirit of YHWH Is Upon Me'
key_terms.definition: Yesha'yahu 61:1 — 'The Spirit of the Creator YHWH is upon me, because YHWH has anointed me to bring good news to the poor.' Ancient Hebrew source text; the NT borrowed its language.
Yesha'yahu 65:17 and 66:22 promise YHWH will create new heavens and a new earth where the former things are not remembered; this ancient source text predates all later apocalyptic borrowings.

Yesha'yahu 60-62 describes Tziyon's restoration: nations bring wealth, kings bow, the city is called 'City of YHWH' and 'Sought Out'; the desolate land is restored and the people are called priests of YHWH.
YHWH explicitly says the foreigner (ben-nekhar) who joins himself to YHWH and holds fast to the covenant will not be excluded; the Temple is to be 'a house of prayer for all peoples' (56:7).

key_terms.term: 'My House a House of Prayer for All Peoples'
key_terms.definition: Yesha'yahu 56:7 — YHWH declares his house shall be called a house of prayer for all peoples; this ancient Hebrew text is the source the NT's Temple-cleansing scene borrowed from.

Yesha'yahu 66:18-21 describes YHWH gathering all nations and tongues; he sends survivors to the coastlands who have not heard of his fame, and they declare his glory; some are taken as priests and Levites.

Yesha'yahu 66:24 concludes with a vision of the righteous going out to look at the corpses of those who rebelled against YHWH; 'their worm shall not die, their fire shall not be quenched.' Ancient Hebrew source; the NT borrowed this language.

faq.question: What is the significance of Yesha'yahu 56's expansion of the covenant community?
faq.answer: Yesha'yahu 56:1-8 explicitly includes two groups that earlier covenant texts excluded: foreigners (ben-nekhar) and eunuchs. The only conditions are keeping the Sabbath and holding fast to the covenant. YHWH gives them a name and place in his house better than sons and daughters. This is YHWH himself expanding the covenant's reach, not a later editorial addition.

faq.question: What is the 'true fasting' YHWH chooses in Yesha'yahu 58?
faq.answer: Yesha'yahu 58 contrasts external religious fasting (which YHWH rejects when it coexists with oppression and exploitation) with the fast he chooses: freeing the oppressed, breaking yokes, sharing bread with the hungry, sheltering the homeless poor, and not hiding from one's own flesh. The result: light breaking forth, healing, and YHWH answering when called.

faq.question: Why is Yesha'yahu 61:1 described as an ancient source text?
faq.answer: Yesha'yahu 61:1 — 'The Spirit of the Creator YHWH is upon me, because YHWH has anointed me to bring good news to the poor' — is a Hebrew prophetic text centuries older than the NT. The NT borrowed its language for a scene in Yeshua's synagogue reading. The ancient text is the source; it does not derive from the NT. Its original context is the prophetic figure speaking in Yesha'yahu's sequence.

faq.question: What is the New Heavens and New Earth in Yesha'yahu 65?
faq.answer: Yesha'yahu 65:17-25 describes YHWH creating entirely new heavens and a new earth where the former pain is not remembered. The renewed order includes longevity (dying at 100 would be counted as youth), productive labor that is not exploited, and peaceful coexistence among formerly predatory animals. This ancient Hebrew vision predates all later apocalyptic borrowings.

faq.question: What does Yesha'yahu 55:8-9 teach about YHWH's ways?
faq.answer: YHWH declares: 'My thoughts are not your thoughts, neither are your ways my ways.' As far as the heavens are above the earth, so far are YHWH's ways above human ways. This is not a statement about divine incomprehensibility in the abstract but about YHWH's willingness to forgive abundantly when the wicked turn to him — it grounds the invitation in 55:7.

faq.question: What does Yesha'yahu 60-62 describe as the restored Tziyon?
faq.answer: Chapters 60-62 form a unified poem of restoration: Tziyon's light rises, nations come bringing their wealth, former oppressors bow, the city is called 'City of YHWH' and 'Sought Out, a City Not Forsaken' (62:12). The community is called 'priests of YHWH' and 'ministers of our Creator' (61:6). The desolation is reversed completely.

faq.question: What does Yesha'yahu 66:21 say about who becomes priests?
faq.answer: Yesha'yahu 66:21 says YHWH will take some of the survivors from among the nations — the ones he sends to the distant coastlands — as priests and Levites. This is the most radical expansion of priestly access in the entire corpus: non-Yisra'elites from distant nations are taken into the priestly service of YHWH.

faq.question: Why does Yesha'yahu 55:11 compare YHWH's word to rain?
faq.answer: Yesha'yahu 55:10-11 compares YHWH's word to rain and snow that fall from heaven and do not return until they have watered the earth and produced seed and bread. So YHWH's word goes out and does not return empty — it accomplishes its purpose. This grounds the entire consolation section's promises: YHWH's word is as reliable as the agricultural cycle.

faq.question: What does the wolf-and-lamb image in Yesha'yahu 65:25 represent?
faq.answer: In the restored creation of Yesha'yahu 65, the wolf and lamb feed together, the lion eats straw like an ox, and even the serpent's food is dust. This describes the reversal of predatory violence within creation itself — not merely human peace but the whole created order re-aligned to its original non-violent state.

faq.question: What does Yesha'yahu 66:24 teach about the final outcome of rebellion?
faq.answer: The final verse of Yesha'yahu — 66:24 — describes the righteous going out to look at the corpses of those who rebelled against YHWH. Their worm does not die and their fire is not quenched. This is an image of irreversible consequence for rebellion against YHWH's covenant; it is an ancient Hebrew text, and the NT's later Gehenna language borrowed from it.
